claims.claim: A presidential veto is the President rejecting legislation, and Congress can override it
claims.sourceSpan: The U.S. Constitution outlines the veto authority in Article I, Section 7.

claims.claim: The President can reject legislation by returning it with objections
claims.sourceSpan: The Constitution states that when the President vetoes a bill,

claims.claim: The override threshold rarely succeeds
claims.section: Summary of Bills Vetoed (112 overridden of 1,533 regular vetoes)

claims.claim: Congress can override with a two-thirds majority in both chambers
claims.sourceSpan: The veto may be overridden by 2/3 vote of both Houses of Congress.

claims.claim: Article I, Section 7 gives the President the power to return legislation with written objections

claims.sourceSpan: Passage by a two-thirds margin in both chambers is required to override a veto before the end of the Congress in which the veto is received.

claims.sourceSpan: A veto threat can also prove to be an effective tool for the President, sometimes forcing Congress to modify legislation before presenting the bill to the President.

claims.claim: CRS: the President "may sign a bill into law within the 10-day period (excluding Sundays)"
claims.sourceSpan: The President may sign a bill into law within the 10-day period (excluding Sundays)

claims.claim: The Constitution directs the President to "return it, with his Objections to that House in which it shall have originated"
claims.sourceSpan: he shall return it, with his Objections to that House in which it shall have originated

claims.claim: A vetoed bill goes back to the chamber it originated in, not to a chamber of the President's choosing; CRS gives the Senate example
claims.sourceSpan: if the President vetoes a bill that was introduced in the Senate, the bill will be returned first to the Senate where the possible override process would begin

claims.claim: CRS calls a returned veto a "regular" or "return" veto
claims.sourceSpan: This type of action is called a "regular" or "return" veto.

claims.claim: A bill not returned within ten days (Sundays excepted) becomes law "in like Manner as if he had signed it"

claims.section: Art. I, sec. 7, par. 2, quoted in the opinion

claims.claim: The exception: "unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law"
claims.sourceSpan: unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law.
claims.section: Art. I, sec. 7, par. 2, quoted in the opinion

claims.claim: If Congress has adjourned within the 10-day period after presentation and the President does not sign, the bill does not become law
claims.sourceSpan: If, on the other hand, Congress has adjourned within the 10-day period after presentation of the bill to the President (thereby preventing the return of the bill to Congress), the President may refuse to sign the bill, and the bill does not become law

claims.claim: CRS: pocket vetoes are "not subject to the congressional veto override process"
claims.sourceSpan: Pocket vetoes are not subject to the congressional veto override process.

claims.claim: The Constitution sets the two-chamber override sequence verbatim
claims.sourceSpan: If after such Reconsideration two thirds of that House shall agree to pass the Bill, it shall be sent, together with the Objections, to the other House, by which it shall likewise be reconsidered, and if approved by two thirds of that House, it shall become a Law.
claims.section: Art. I, sec. 7, par. 2, quoted in the opinion

claims.claim: The originating chamber votes first, and the second chamber votes only if the first reaches two-thirds
claims.sourceSpan: If a two-thirds vote is successful in the originating chamber, that chamber informs the other of its decision to override the veto by message.

claims.claim: Two-thirds means two-thirds of Members PRESENT AND VOTING, provided a quorum is present
claims.sourceSpan: congressional procedure, tradition, and judicial rulings have interpreted this requirement to mean two thirds of those Members present and voting, provided there is a quorum present

claims.claim: Neither chamber is obliged to schedule an override vote at all
claims.sourceSpan: Neither chamber is under any constitutional, legal, or procedural obligation to schedule an override vote. It is not unusual for Congress to make no effort to override the veto if congressional leaders do not believe they have sufficient votes.

claims.claim: An override must be completed before the end of the Congress in which the veto is received
claims.sourceSpan: before the end of the Congress in which the veto is received

claims.claim: REJECTED — the Phase A sweep graded the veto tally an F-FAIL "fabricated-statistics class" error, reporting that the American Presidency Project says 1,497 regular / 1,099 pocket / 2,596 total / 111 overridden. It does not. Three independent authorities give exactly the published figures: the Senate summary table's own Total row (1533/1066/2599/112); the APP table summed from its own 47 per-president rows (identical); and CRS RS22188, whose July 2019 counts (1,510 / 1,066 / 2,576 / 111) roll forward to the same numbers once Trump I's remaining 8 regular vetoes and 1 override, Biden's 13 and Trump II's 2 are added. The sweep's four numbers appear nowhere in the stored APP page. Every published figure was CORRECT; the real defect was that the sentence carried no attribution and no as-of date.

REMOVED: "The President returns the bill to the originating chamber - typically the House". No stored source states which chamber is typical, and RS22188's own worked example is a Senate-originated bill. Replaced with the constitutional rule plus CRS's example.

REMOVED: "The Constitution requires the message be transmitted; a veto without written objections would be constitutionally irregular." The second half is speculation about a hypothetical no stored source addresses.
REMOVED: "Presidents occasionally let bills become law this way to signal displeasure without formally rejecting them." Motive claim, unsourced in every stored file.

REMOVED: "Two-thirds of the House present and voting means approximately 290 votes when all members are present. Two-thirds of the Senate means 67 votes." Neither chamber size nor the derived counts is in any stored source, and stating fixed vote counts is the exact confusion RS22188 footnote 7 exists to correct - the threshold is two-thirds of those present and voting, provided a quorum, so it moves with attendance. Replaced with the sourced rule.
REMOVED: "the override attempt fails and the veto stands without a Senate vote." True only when the House originated the bill. Replaced with "the second chamber never votes."

REMOVED in full: "A bill passed over a veto threat can still serve political purposes - it puts the President on record as opposing something popular, creates an issue for the next election, or pressures the President to negotiate. But it rarely becomes law. The strategic value of forcing a veto is usually messaging, not legislation." Four consecutive unsourced motive and strategy claims.

REMOVED: "The veto's more common function is as a constraint on what Congress passes, rather than an actual block on enacted legislation." A comparative frequency claim with nothing behind it. The sourced version of the same point - RS22188's veto-signaling passage - now opens that section.
REMOVED: "It becomes law on the date of signature, or the effective date specified in the bill if different." No stored source addresses effective dates.

REMOVED the word "enrolled" from "the bill is enrolled and transmitted to the President". RS22188 uses "presented"; the only stored description of enrollment is IF10515's NDAA-specific sentence, which is an example rather than a general rule.

REPLACED: "the veto threat alone functions as a powerful tool that shapes legislation" with RS22188's own characterisation ("an effective tool ... sometimes forcing Congress to modify legislation before presenting the bill to the President").

ADDED, sourced: the Line Item Veto Act was never limited to spending. The article said "specific provisions of spending bills"; the Court's own description lists three categories, one of which is limited tax benefits, and one of the two cancellations before the Court was a tax provision.
ADDED, sourced: "provided there is a quorum present" - a condition RS22188 footnote 7 states and the article had dropped.
ADDED, sourced: neither chamber is obliged to hold an override vote at all (RS22188).
ADDED, sourced: the ~7% all-time override rate understates the modern rate; CRS's 1961-forward count is 245 regular vetoes and 38 overridden (15.5%), bounded to its July 2019 edition.

ADDED to the Key Sources box and the JSON-LD citation array: CRS RS22188, the American Presidency Project veto table, and a working link for Clinton v. City of New York. The page previously cited two URLs for an article resting on figures neither of them was used to check.

notes:
First-refresh audit of a May 2026 pre-lane explainer, Phase B session 7 (veto cluster) of the article audit sweep.

THE SWEEP'S HEADLINE FINDING WAS FALSE AND IS REJECTED ON THE RECORD. Phase A graded this page's veto tally an F-FAIL of the fabricated-statistics class, reporting that the American Presidency Project gives 1,497 regular / 1,099 pocket / 2,596 total / 111 overridden against the article's 1,533 / 1,066 / 2,599 / 112. Three independent authorities were fetched and stored, and all three give the article's figures: the Senate's own summary table carries them in its Total row; the APP table, summed from its own 47 per-president rows (43 Totals rows plus Harding, who has none), returns the identical four numbers; and CRS RS22188's July 2019 counts of 1,510 / 1,066 / 2,576 / 111 roll forward to exactly the published figures once Trump I's remaining regular vetoes and one override, Biden's 13 and Trump II's 2 are added. The sweep's four numbers appear nowhere in the stored APP page. Every published figure was correct. The real defect was that the sentence cited nothing and carried no as-of date, and that is what was fixed.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG. Nine claim families removed rather than softened: 'typically the House' as the chamber a veto returns to (no source states which is typical, and CRS's own worked example is a Senate-originated bill); the speculation that a veto without written objections 'would be constitutionally irregular'; the motive claim that presidents let bills lapse into law 'to signal displeasure'; the fixed vote counts 'approximately 290' and '67', which are the exact confusion RS22188 footnote 7 exists to correct, since the threshold is two thirds of those present and voting provided a quorum and therefore moves with attendance; 'without a Senate vote', true only when the House originated the bill; a four-sentence paragraph of unsourced motive and strategy about the messaging value of forcing a veto; the comparative-frequency claim that the veto's 'more common function' is as a constraint; an effective-date gloss on signing; and the word 'enrolled', for which the only stored description is an NDAA-specific sentence.

ADDED, ALL SOURCED: the quorum condition RS22188 states and the article had dropped; CRS's statement that neither chamber is obliged to schedule an override vote at all; the modern override rate (245 regular vetoes and 38 overridden, 15.5%, since 1961, bounded to the July 2019 edition) which corrects the impression the all-time 7% leaves; the six-quotation SAP passage; and the fact that the Line Item Veto Act was never confined to spending - the Court's own description lists dollar amounts of discretionary budget authority, items of new direct spending AND limited tax benefits, and the Snake River cancellation before the Court was a tax provision.

CONVERGENCE: two rounds. Round 1 REFUSED. Its single material finding was one this rewrite had itself introduced: the deleted comparative-frequency sentence had been replaced with a NEW unsourced proportion claim opening the negotiating-tool section. Four smaller items came with it, including a Clinton v. City of New York holding quoted from the Reporter of Decisions' syllabus rather than from the opinion. All five fixed. Round 2 on the frozen file SIGNED OFF, having independently re-derived all four tally figures twice (summing the Senate table's 47 rows, and summing the APP table separately), located the holding quotation in the opinion rather than the syllabus, checked every quotation character by character, and cross-checked the page against the pocket-veto draft for factual collision. Two cosmetic residuals it raised were also fixed.

Also corrected in passing: nine quotations carried a period or comma inside the closing quote mark that the source sentence does not carry, so nine receipts would not have resolved.
